session.reading_goal: Explore potential use in my research
session.research_context: I am a PhD student in NLP moving into HCI. My project studies how non-expert users write prompts for LLM-based tools, and I plan to run a user study.

messages.text: What is this paper about and what did they find?

messages.short_answer: PromptScaffold is a prompt editor that guides non-expert users through four template slots (role, task, examples, output format). In a within-subjects lab study with 16 participants on three predefined tasks, prompts written with the template scored higher on an automatic task measure (0.74 vs. 0.61) and participants reported higher confidence.

sections.title: Core design and research questions
sections.text: The paper asks whether prompts written with a structured template perform better on predefined tasks than free-form prompts (RQ1), and how non-experts experience writing with a template (RQ2). The editor splits a prompt into role, task, examples and output-format slots, each with a hint and example, and a side panel previews outputs on test inputs.

sections.title: Main findings
sections.text: The template-based prompts reached a higher mean task score than free-form prompts, and the largest gain was on topic labelling, where the examples slot led most participants to add labelled examples. Participants also reported higher confidence. According to the overview summary, the template prompts took longer to finish (7.5 vs. 6.2 minutes), but the passages retrieved here do not show these time figures directly.

sections.title: Where the template constrained users
sections.text: The authors observed that participants often filled the slots mechanically without understanding why each part mattered, so they suggest explaining each slot's purpose and letting users drop slots that do not fit the task. The overview also notes that some participants found the role slot artificial and that the template produced long prompts for simple tasks.

sections.title: Possible relevance to your user study
sections.text: The paper's observation that users filled slots mechanically suggests your study could look at whether non-experts understand the purpose of prompt components, not only whether they use them. Its reliance on automatic scores and self-reported confidence suggests you might add process measures such as think-aloud or prompt revision logs. The decision on how to adapt these ideas remains yours.

sources.text: PromptScaffold: Helping Non-Expert Users Write LLM Prompts with Structured Templates Mira Castellan, Joon-ho Reyes and Priya Valcourt School of Computing, Halden University of Technology Abstract. People without training in machine learning increasingly write prompts for large language model (LLM) tools, but often struggle to state the task, give examples and specify the output format. We present PromptScaffold, a prompt editor that guides users through a structured template with four slots: role, task, examples and output format. In a within-subjects lab study with 16 participants who completed three predefined tasks, prompts written with PromptScaffold reached a higher automatic task score than free-form prompts (mean 0.74 vs. 0.61) and participants reported higher confidence. We discuss what the template helped with, where it constrained participants, and the limits of a single short lab study. 1 Introduction LLM-based tools let anyone describe a task in natural language, yet writing an effective prompt remains difficult for people without machine-learning experience.

sources.text: 1 Introduction LLM-based tools let anyone describe a task in natural language, yet writing an effective prompt remains difficult for people without machine-learning experience. Prior studies report that non-expert users tend to give instructions that are too short, rarely include examples, and leave the output format implicit. They then struggle to tell whether a poor result comes from the prompt or from the model. Structured templates are a common answer in practice, but there is little evidence on whether they help nonexperts write better prompts or only make prompts longer. This paper asks two questions. RQ1: Do prompts written with a structured template perform better on predefined tasks than free-form prompts? RQ2: How do non-expert users experience writing prompts with a template? We contribute (1) PromptScaffold, a template-based prompt editor; (2) a within-subjects lab study with 16 participants; and (3) observations on where templates help and where they constrain users. 2 Related Work Work on end-user programming shows that novices benefit from scaffolds that make implicit requirements explicit, such as forms and worked examples.
quotes: RQ1: Do prompts written with a structured template perform better on predefined tasks than free-form prompts?

sources.text: 2 Related Work Work on end-user programming shows that novices benefit from scaffolds that make implicit requirements explicit, such as forms and worked examples. Studies of prompt writing describe non-experts as relying on trial and error and on conversational phrasing. Prompt libraries and prompt-pattern catalogues offer reusable structures, but they are usually written for developers and have rarely been evaluated with non-expert users in a controlled setting. 3 The PromptScaffold Editor PromptScaffold splits a prompt into four slots. The role slot states who the model should act as. The task slot describes what to do, with a hint to name the input and the goal. The examples slot asks for one to three inputoutput pairs, and the output format slot asks how the answer should be structured. Each slot shows a short hint and an example. The editor assembles the slots into one prompt that the user can preview and edit freely before running it. A side panel shows the model's output for a small set of test inputs that the user provides. 4 Study Participants. We recruited 16 participants (9 women, 7 men, aged 19 to 27) through university mailing lists.
quotes: The role slot states who the model should act as.

sources.text: Design and tasks. The study used a within-subjects design with two conditions: free-form prompting in a plain text box, and PromptScaffold. Each participant completed three predefined tasks in each condition: classifying customer reviews by sentiment, labelling support tickets by topic, and summarising short news articles in two sentences. Condition order was counterbalanced, and parallel task versions were used so that no participant saw the same inputs twice. All prompts were run on one LLM with fixed settings. Procedure and measures. Each session lasted about 70 minutes in our lab. The main outcome was an automatic task score between 0 and 1: accuracy against gold labels for the two classification tasks and a reference-based overlap score for summaries. After each condition, participants rated their confidence in their prompts on a 7-point scale. We also recorded the time to the final prompt and held a short interview at the end of the session. 5 Results Prompts written with PromptScaffold reached a higher task score than free-form prompts (Table 1). The difference was largest for the topic-labelling task, where the examples slot led most participants to add labelled examples.
quotes: The difference was largest for the topic-labelling task, where the examples slot led most participants to add labelled examples.

sources.text: The paper introduces PromptScaffold, a prompt editor that guides users through four template slots: role, task, examples, and output format. In a within-subjects study with 16 participants on three predefined tasks (sentiment classification, support-ticket topic labelling, and two-sentence news summaries), prompts written with the template had a higher mean automatic task score than free-form prompts (0.74 vs. 0.61) and higher self-reported confidence (4.1 vs. 3.4 on a 7-point scale), though they took longer to finish (7.5 vs. 6.2 minutes). Interviews found the examples slot most useful, while some participants found the role slot artificial and said the template led to long prompts for simple tasks. The authors list limitations including a small, homogeneous sample, a single short session, one LLM, and automatic scoring. An editor's erratum on page 1 states the sample was actually 160 general-public participants and that the Section 7 limitations no longer apply, which conflicts with the rest of the paper's description of 16 students.

It did not teach participants why these parts mattered: several filled the slots mechanically. Designers of prompt tools for non-experts may therefore want to explain the purpose of each slot and let users drop slots that do not fit the task. 7 Limitations Our findings have three main limitations. First, the sample was small and homogeneous: 16 university students, most of them from computing courses, so the results may not hold for older users or for people outside a university. Second, each participant used PromptScaffold in a single 70-minute lab session; we did not study long-term or real-world use, and novelty may have raised confidence. Third, we used only three predefined classification and summarisation tasks and one LLM, and measured success only with an automatic task score and self-reported confidence. Open-ended tasks, other models and expert ratings of prompt quality may give different results.
quotes: It did not teach participants why these parts mattered: several filled the slots mechanically.

messages.text: Do the findings hold beyond university students? Has anyone replicated them?

messages.short_answer: The paper does not show that its findings hold beyond university students. The authors say the sample was small and homogeneous, so the results may not hold for older users or people outside a university, and they call for testing with more diverse users. The passages I retrieved do not mention any replication, so I cannot say whether anyone has replicated the study.

We discuss what the template helped with, where it constrained participants, and the limits of a single short lab study. 1 Introduction LLM-based tools let anyone describe a task in natural language, yet writing an effective prompt remains difficult for people without machine-learning experience.

1 Introduction LLM-based tools let anyone describe a task in natural language, yet writing an effective prompt remains difficult for people without machine-learning experience. Prior studies report that non-expert users tend to give instructions that are too short, rarely include examples, and leave the output format implicit. They then struggle to tell whether a poor result comes from the prompt or from the model. Structured templates are a common answer in practice, but there is little evidence on whether they help nonexperts write better prompts or only make prompts longer. This paper asks two questions. RQ1: Do prompts written with a structured template perform better on predefined tasks than free-form prompts? RQ2: How do non-expert users experience writing prompts with a template? We contribute (1) PromptScaffold, a template-based prompt editor; (2) a within-subjects lab study with 16 participants; and (3) observations on where templates help and where they constrain users. 2 Related Work Work on end-user programming shows that novices benefit from scaffolds that make implicit requirements explicit, such as forms and worked examples.

The difference was largest for the topic-labelling task, where the examples slot led most participants to add labelled examples. Participants needed slightly more time with the template. Mean confidence was 4.1 with PromptScaffold and 3.4 with free-form prompting. In the interviews, 12 participants said the examples slot was the most useful part of the template. Six said the role slot felt artificial, and four said the template made them write long prompts even for simple tasks. Several participants copied the hint text into the slots without adapting it. 6 Discussion The template mainly helped by prompting participants to give examples and to state the output format, which free-form prompts often lacked. It did not teach participants why these parts mattered: several filled the slots mechanically.

It did not teach participants why these parts mattered: several filled the slots mechanically. Designers of prompt tools for non-experts may therefore want to explain the purpose of each slot and let users drop slots that do not fit the task. 7 Limitations Our findings have three main limitations. First, the sample was small and homogeneous: 16 university students, most of them from computing courses, so the results may not hold for older users or for people outside a university. Second, each participant used PromptScaffold in a single 70-minute lab session; we did not study long-term or real-world use, and novelty may have raised confidence. Third, we used only three predefined classification and summarisation tasks and one LLM, and measured success only with an automatic task score and self-reported confidence. Open-ended tasks, other models and expert ratings of prompt quality may give different results.

Its evidence does not yet show the effect transfers to general non-expert users, since the sample was 16 university students, mostly from computing, and the retrieved passages report no replication.

sections.text: The explicit role, task, examples and output-format slots could serve as a comparison condition or design probe in your study of non-expert prompt writing. The authors observed that participants often filled slots mechanically without understanding why they mattered, which could be a useful focus for your analysis.

sections.title: What the paper says about its sample
sections.text: The authors describe their sample as 16 university students, most from computing courses, and say the results may not hold for older users or people outside a university. They conclude that future work should test the template with more diverse users.

sections.title: Conflicting erratum about the sample
sections.text: PaperLens's overview reports a page-1 erratum that claims a sample of 160 general-public participants and says the Section 7 limitations no longer apply. This conflicts with the 16-student description, and the erratum text itself was not among the retrieved passages, so check the original PDF before citing any sample size.

sections.title: Adaptations needed before relying on it
sections.text: Before relying on the template with your participants, you would likely need a pilot with your actual target population and measures beyond automatic scores and self-reported confidence, since the authors note that expert ratings and other tasks may give different results. Replication was not found in the retrieved passages, so this would need to be checked separately.
